Class CausalCoordination

java.lang.Object
io.github.tobyjamesclements.parsley.CausalCoordination
public final class CausalCoordination extends Object
The public handle that turns on topology-epoch coordination for a causal application. Create one, register it with every CausalProcessors / CausalStreams builder whose stages should participate (via withCoordination(...)), and close it from your shutdown path — the same shape as CausalQuiesce: 
CausalCoordination coordination = CausalCoordination.create("parsley-epoch-events");

Topology topology = CausalStreams.builder(userSupplier)
        .addBufferStore("parsley", CausalBufferLimit.ofDuration(limit))
        .addSource(CausalBuffer.of("prices", Serdes.String(), priceSerde))
        .addSink("enriched", "enriched-output", Serdes.String(), enrichedSerde)
        .withCoordination(coordination)   // "prices" is derived as an external source; "enriched-output" a sink
        .build();

KafkaStreams streams = new KafkaStreams(topology, props);
streams.start();
// ... to evolve the running topology through an epoch boundary:
coordination.requestEpochTransition();
// ... in shutdown, after streams.close():
coordination.close();

Without a CausalCoordination, a topology runs in epoch 0 exactly as before: no epoch-events log, no coordination thread, every coordination path inert.

What it owns. One ParsleyEpochRuntime per application instance — the deterministic fold over the shared epochEventsTopic log plus the round-owner runtime. It is built lazily at the first participating task's init(), because only then is the task's appConfigs() (broker + security) available for the runtime's raw Kafka clients; every later task on the instance shares the same runtime.

Thread-safety: safe to share across every task's Kafka Streams thread and to call requestEpochTransition() / close() from an unrelated thread.

  • Method Details

    • create

      public static CausalCoordination create(String epochEventsTopic)
      Creates a coordination handle over the shared epochEventsTopic log. The topology's external source topics — the entry-point topics produced by systems outside the topology, on which no in-band epoch marker ever arrives — are derived from the log: every participating stage declares its input channels and sink topics on join, and a topic some member consumes but no member produces is an external source (so a stage consuming one self-initiates the wave and adopts that coordinate's floor from the log). Declare sink topics via CausalStreams.addSink(...) — which does so automatically — or CausalProcessors.Builder.sinkTopics(...) on the low-level path.
      Parameters:
      epochEventsTopic - the single-partition epoch-events log topic name
      Returns:
      a new coordination handle

    • create

      public static CausalCoordination create(String epochEventsTopic, CausalMembershipStrategy membershipStrategy)
      As create(String), with an explicit CausalMembershipStrategy governing how an epoch transition treats a member that has not published. The default CausalMembershipStrategy.blockUntilDrained() blocks the transition until every member publishes.
      Parameters:
      epochEventsTopic - the single-partition epoch-events log topic name
      membershipStrategy - how a blocked round treats members that have not published
      Returns:
      a new coordination handle

    • requestEpochTransition

      public void requestEpochTransition()
      Requests an epoch transition across the currently-running nodes: opens a snapshot round attributed to a local running member so this instance owns and commits it. The running nodes publish their frontiers, the owner merge-mins them into the new floor, and the boundary propagates in-band.
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if no task has initialised coordination yet, or no local member has joined (so there is nothing to attribute the request to)

    • leave

      public void leave()
      Gracefully decommissions this instance's members from the epoch domain — a genuine removal, not a restart (a restart must not call this: leaving it out lets the member stay in the domain and return with no epoch churn). Blocking, in three phases, honouring "only a drained node is excluded":
      1. Drain. Waits — unbounded, no timeout — until every local member's causal buffer is empty, so removing them strands no held record. The task threads keep delivering meanwhile; the buffer drains through the ordinary path as dependencies arrive.
      2. Remove. Appends a Leave for each local member and waits until the fold has dropped them from the running set, so the departure is durable on the log.
      3. Re-settle. Requests a new epoch over the remaining members — the leaver excluded, since its Leave precedes the request in log order — then returns without waiting for that epoch to commit, so shutdown is never coupled to the remaining members' liveness (the survivors commit it on their own).
      A no-op if no task has initialised coordination or no local member has joined. Contract: the caller must have stopped feeding this node new input before decommissioning — leave() drains the in-flight buffer, not records that arrive after it returns.

    • close

      public void close()
      Stops the coordination runtime (its poll thread and Kafka clients). Idempotent; call it from your shutdown path after KafkaStreams#close. A no-op if no task ever initialised coordination.
